item.title: Water Lilies
item.lesson: Monet's final revolution began as gardening. Prosperous at last after decades of poverty, he bought his house at Giverny, diverted a stream (over his neighbors' protests), planted exotic water lilies, and built a Japanese footbridge in homage to the woodblock prints he collected — then spent thirty years painting what he had grown. By 1906 he had made the decisive cut: the horizon is gone. No sky, no shore, no bridge — only the pond's surface, where floating blossoms and reflected clouds share a single plane and you can no longer say which direction is up. He exhibited forty-eight of these 'water landscapes' in 1909 and the series consumed him for the rest of his life, through failing eyesight and cataract surgery, culminating in the vast murals he gave France. The garden was the first draft; the paintings drifted so close to pure abstraction that the Abstract Expressionists later claimed Monet as one of their own.
item.lookFor: Try to find where the water's surface actually is — Monet gives you lily pads (on it), reflected sky (in it), and depths (under it), and lets your eye assemble the plane from evidence.
